title: Straight stitch
subtitle: A single flat stitch placed in any direction to form spokes, rays or scattered fillings
excerpt: Straight stitch is the most basic embroidery stitch: one stitch placed in any angle or length to form a single mark. Groups of straight stitches can radiate as flower petals, scatter as a light filling, or fan as leaf veins. It is the foundation from which many composite stitches are built.
sourceNotes: Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), flat stitches section (Project Gutenberg #20776). Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882). Mrs Beeton, Book of Needlework (1870).

content.text: Straight stitch is a single flat stitch that can be placed in any direction and at any length. It belongs to the flat stitch family and is one of the most fundamental marks in surface embroidery. Used on its own it forms spokes and rays; arranged in tight groups it fills small shapes; scattered at random angles it creates light texture. Many built-up stitches, from woven wheels to star fillings, are made from straight stitches arranged in a pattern.

items.label: Thread
items.value: Stranded cotton, 2 or 3 strands depending on the weight of mark needed

content.text: Secure the thread on the back and bring the needle up at point A, the start (inner end) of the stitch.

Lay the thread in the direction required and insert the needle down at point B, the end (outer tip) of the stitch. The length can be anything from 2 mm to about 2 cm; longer straight stitches tend to snag in use.
Pull the thread through at an even tension. The stitch should lie flat on the fabric without puckering. If the fabric pulls, the stitch is too tight.

To place the next stitch, bring the needle up at the new point A for that stitch. When making a radiating group (such as a simple flower), bring all stitches up near a central point and take them down at the outer edge, spacing them evenly around the shape.
When the shape is filled or the group is complete, fasten off the thread on the back.

items.symptom: The fabric puckers under the stitches
items.cause: The thread has been pulled too tight
items.fix: After pulling the thread through, ease it so it lies on the surface of the fabric rather than biting into it. Working in a hoop helps keep the fabric taut so you can judge tension accurately.

items.symptom: Long stitches catch and distort in use
items.cause: Stitches are too long for the thread weight
items.fix: Keep individual straight stitches under 2 cm. For larger areas, use a filling stitch such as seed stitch or satin stitch instead of one very long stitch.
